        <p class="section-lede" data-reveal data-reveal-delay="1">Students should leave a course able to build—but also able to ask whether a system should be built, how it can fail, and who carries the consequences.</p>

        <div class="teaching-card" data-reveal><span class="card-index">01 / FIRST PRINCIPLES</span><h3 class="card-title" style="margin-top: 2rem">Reason before recipes</h3><p class="card-copy">Models become durable knowledge when students understand assumptions, geometry, uncertainty, and tradeoffs—not just function calls.</p></div>
        <div class="teaching-card" data-reveal data-reveal-delay="1"><span class="card-index">02 / PRACTICE</span><h3 class="card-title" style="margin-top: 2rem">Build the whole path</h3><p class="card-copy">Git, environments, cleaning, modeling, testing, deployment, monitoring, and communication belong in the same learning journey.</p></div>
        <div class="teaching-card" data-reveal data-reveal-delay="2"><span class="card-index">03 / RESPONSIBILITY</span><h3 class="card-title" style="margin-top: 2rem">Make failure visible</h3><p class="card-copy">Students examine privacy, leakage, bias, hallucination, and evaluation gaps as engineering realities—not footnotes.</p></div>
